                                   6                                           SAN JOSE DIVISION

                                   8        MICHAEL ESKENASY,                                 Case No. 26-cv-06047-VKD
                                                         Plaintiff,                           ORDER GRANTING APPLICATION
                                   9
                                                                                              TO PROCEED IN FORMA PAUPERIS;
                                                   v.                                         STAYING SERVICE OF PROCESS;
                                  10
                                                                                              AND SCREENING COMPLAINT
                                  11        LINKEDIN CORPORATION, et al.,                     PURSUANT TO 28 U.S.C. § 1915
                                                         Defendants.                          Re: Dkt. Nos. 1, 2
                                  12
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13

                                  14            On June 18, 2026, plaintiff Michael Eskenasy, who is representing himself, filed a

                                  15   complaint and application to proceed in forma pauperis (“IFP”). Dkt. Nos. 1, 2.

                                  16            The Court grants Mr. Eskenasy’s IFP application. Having screened Mr. Eskenasy’s

                                  17   complaint pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e), however, the Court finds that the complaint fails to

                                  18   state sufficient facts supporting federal subject matter jurisdiction and fails to state a claim for

                                  19   relief. The Court stays service of process and gives Mr. Eskenasy until August 7, 2026 to file an

                                  20   amended complaint that addresses the deficiencies identified in this order. If Mr. Eskenasy fails to

                                  21   file an amended complaint in time, or if the amended complaint fails to cure the defects described

                                  22   in this order, the Court may issue an order reassigning the case to a district judge with a

                                  23   recommendation that the complaint be dismissed for lack of federal subject matter jurisdiction and

                                  24   failure to state a claim.

                                  25   I.       IFP APPLICATION
                                  26            A court may allow a plaintiff to prosecute an action in federal court without prepayment of

                                  27   fees or security if the plaintiff submits an affidavit showing that he or she is unable to pay such

                                  28   fees or provide such security. See 28 U.S.C. § 1915(a). A court may dismiss a case filed without
                                          Case 5:26-cv-06047-VKD              Document 5        Filed 07/08/26     Page 2 of 7




                                   1   the payment of the filing fee whenever it determines that the action “(i) is frivolous or malicious;

                                   2   (ii) fails to state a claim on which relief may be granted; or (iii) seeks monetary relief against a

                                   3   defendant who is immune from such relief.” 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(i)-(iii). The screening

                                   4   requirement of § 1915(e) applies to all in forma pauperis complaints, not just those filed by

                                   5   prisoners. Calhoun v. Stahl, 254 F.3d 845 (9th Cir. 2001) (“[T]he provisions of 28 U.S.C.

                                   6   § 1915(e)(2)(B) are not limited to prisoners.”); Castro v. Pascual, No. 20-cv-01090-BLF, 2020

                                   7   WL 733127, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 13, 2020) (same).

                                   8           Mr. Eskenasy’s IFP application indicates that he satisfies the economic eligibility

                                   9   requirement of 28 U.S.C. § 1915. The Court therefore grants his IFP application.

                                  10   II.     REVIEW OF COMPLAINT
                                  11           A.      Legal Standard
                                  12           While pro se pleadings are liberally construed, a complaint does not state a claim if it fails
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   to set forth “enough facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.” Bell Atl. Corp. v.

                                  14   Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007); see also Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6). A complaint must include

                                  15   facts that are “more than labels and conclusions, and formulaic recitation of the elements of a

                                  16   cause of action will not do.” Twombly, 550 U.S. at 555. “Threadbare recitals of the elements of a

                                  17   cause of action, supported by mere conclusory statements, do not suffice.” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556

                                  18   U.S. 662, 678 (2009). Only plausible claims for relief will survive a motion to dismiss. Id. at 679.

                                  19   A claim is plausible if the facts pled permit the court to draw a reasonable inference that the

                                  20   defendant is liable for the alleged misconduct. Id.

                                  21           As a threshold matter, the Court must examine whether it has jurisdiction over the claims

                                  22   alleged before considering whether the complaint states any claims on which relief may be

                                  23   granted. See Sinochem Int’l Co. v. Malaysia Int’l Shipping Corp., 549 U.S. 422, 430-31

                                  24   (2007) (“[A] federal court generally may not rule on the merits of a case without first determining

                                  25   that it has jurisdiction over the category of claim in suit (subject-matter jurisdiction) and the

                                  26   parties (personal jurisdiction).”).

                                  27           B.      Mr. Eskenasy’s Claims
                                  28           According to the complaint, Mr. Eskenasy is the “founder and architect of ChefreyOS, a
                                                                                           2
                                          Case 5:26-cv-06047-VKD           Document 5          Filed 07/08/26    Page 3 of 7




                                   1   Human Cognitive Infrastructure system and body of work focused on context preservation,

                                   2   coordination, memory, judgment, professional execution, and the operational problem created by

                                   3   fragmented digital tools and platforms.” Dkt. No. 1 ¶ 3. Defendants are LinkedIn Corporation

                                   4   (“LinkedIn”), Microsoft Corporation (“Microsoft”), and 25 Doe defendants. Id. ¶¶ 21-27. Mr.

                                   5   Eskenasy alleges that he “observed third-party LinkedIn content that appeared relevant to

                                   6   authorship, provenance, framework, terminology, language, or comparison issues involving

                                   7   ChefreyOS and Human Cognitive Infrastructure.” Id. ¶ 5. Mr. Eskenasy alleges that the record

                                   8   “raises a serious authorship/provenance concern.” Id. ¶ 8.

                                   9          Mr. Eskenasy further alleges that when he “attempted to address the authorship/provenance

                                  10   concern, [p]laintiff encountered LinkedIn account-access friction.” Id. ¶ 66. Specifically, Mr.

                                  11   Eskenasy claims that LinkedIn temporarily restricted his access to his LinkedIn account and made

                                  12   him undergo “a security check” and “identity verification as a condition of account access.” See
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   id. ¶¶ 67-74. He further alleges that he encountered errors when attempting to verify his identity.

                                  14   Id. ¶¶ 75-79. Mr. Eskenasy alleges that LinkedIn’s identity verification process “imposed a

                                  15   sensitive burden on [p]laintiff and created a barrier to account access.” Id. ¶ 83.

                                  16          According to the complaint, Mr. Eskenasy “does not allege at this stage that copying, theft,

                                  17   misappropriation, retaliation, suppression, or intentional misconduct has already been proven,”

                                  18   and he “does not allege as established fact that LinkedIn intentionally suppressed, shadow-banned,

                                  19   or visibility-limited [p]laintiff.” Id. ¶¶ 7, 86; see also id. ¶¶ 190-200. Rather, Mr. Eskenasy

                                  20   claims that he “brings this action to preserve the record” and that LinkedIn’s and Microsoft’s

                                  21   records are “necessary to determine what happened.” Id. ¶¶ 8, 16. Mr. Eskenasy alleges that

                                  22   Microsoft, as the parent or corporate affiliate of LinkedIn, “may possess, control, receive, govern,

                                  23   supervise, access, or have remediation authority over relevant LinkedIn systems, data, records,

                                  24   policies, affiliate systems, infrastructure, account systems, identity-verification systems, legal

                                  25   systems, support systems, or platform governance.” Id. ¶ 23.

                                  26          The complaint asserts ten claims: (1) breach of contract against LinkedIn; (2) breach of

                                  27   implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing against LinkedIn; (3) violation of California’s

                                  28   unfair competition law, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200, against LinkedIn and Microsoft; (4)
                                                                                          3
                                            Case 5:26-cv-06047-VKD          Document 5       Filed 07/08/26      Page 4 of 7




                                   1   declaratory relief against LinkedIn and Microsoft; (5) injunctive and equitable relief against

                                   2   LinkedIn and Microsoft; (6) equitable record review/accounting/preservation against LinkedIn and

                                   3   Microsoft; (7) negligent platform process/negligent handling against LinkedIn; (8)

                                   4   negligence/equitable relief regarding identity-verification process against LinkedIn and Doe

                                   5   defendants; (9) business, professional, and reputational harm according to proof against LinkedIn

                                   6   and Microsoft; and (10) protection of confidential ChefreyOS materials. Id. at 6-10.

                                   7           Mr. Eskenasy seeks damages, declaratory relief, injunctive relief, and pre- and post-

                                   8   judgment interest. Id. at 10-11.1

                                   9           C.     Subject Matter Jurisdiction
                                  10           For a case to proceed in federal court, the Court must have subject matter jurisdiction over

                                  11   the claims alleged. “It is a fundamental precept that federal courts are courts of limited

                                  12   jurisdiction.” Owen Equip. & Erection Co. v. Kroger, 437 U.S. 365, 374 (1978); see also Ngoc
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Lam Che v. San Jose/Evergreen Cmty. Coll. Dist. Found., No. 17-cv-00381-BLF, 2017 WL

                                  14   2954647, at *2 (N.D. Cal. July 11, 2017) (“Limits upon federal jurisdiction must not be

                                  15   disregarded or evaded.”).

                                  16           Mr. Eskenasy asserts that the Court has jurisdiction in this matter under 28 U.S.C. § 1332

                                  17   (diversity jurisdiction) and 28 U.S.C. § 1367 (supplemental jurisdiction). Federal district courts

                                  18   have diversity jurisdiction over civil actions in which the matter in controversy exceeds the sum or

                                  19   value of $75,000 (exclusive of interest and costs) and is between citizens of different states. 28

                                  20   U.S.C. § 1332(a). “The party seeking to invoke the district court’s diversity jurisdiction always

                                  21   bears the burden of both pleading and proving diversity jurisdiction.” NewGen, LLC v. Safe Cig,

                                  22   LLC, 840 F.3d 606, 613-14 (9th Cir. 2016).

                                  23           The complaint does not allege sufficient facts to establish diversity jurisdiction. First, Mr.

                                  24   Eskenasy alleges that he is a citizen of Idaho and that LinkedIn and Microsoft are not citizens of

                                  25   Idaho. Dkt. No. 1 ¶¶ 31-32. However, as Mr. Eskenasy does not affirmatively allege the

                                  26   citizenship of LinkedIn or Microsoft, he has not adequately alleged diversity of citizenship. See

                                  27
                                       1
                                  28     The “initial exhibit list/evidence preservation index” filed with the complaint refers to exhibits
                                       that were not, in fact, filed with the Court. See Dkt. No. 1 at 11; Dkt. No. 1-1.
                                                                                           4
                                          Case 5:26-cv-06047-VKD            Document 5         Filed 07/08/26     Page 5 of 7




                                   1   Kanter v. Warner-Lambert Co., 265 F.3d 853, 857 (9th Cir. 2001) (“Absent unusual

                                   2   circumstances, a party seeking to invoke diversity jurisdiction should be able to allege

                                   3   affirmatively the actual citizenship of the relevant parties.”); see also Fan v. Cal. Univ. - Silicon

                                   4   Valley, No. 25-cv-07860-VKD, 2025 WL 3068072, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 3, 2025) (finding that

                                   5   plaintiff failed to establish diversity jurisdiction because she did “not allege the citizenship of each

                                   6   of the parties”).

                                   7           Second, the complaint does not contain any factual allegations regarding the amount in

                                   8   controversy. While Mr. Eskenasy alleges that the “amount in controversy exceeds $75,000,” see

                                   9   Dkt. No. 1 ¶¶ 30, 33, these allegations are conclusory and do not provide any factual basis from

                                  10   which the Court may infer that Mr. Eskenasy has satisfied the amount-in-controversy requirement.

                                  11   See Watters v. Parviz, No. 23-35601, 2024 WL 5423073, at *3 (9th Cir. Feb. 21, 2025) (plaintiff’s

                                  12   speculation “that ‘special and punitive damages could be well into the hundreds of thousands of
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   dollars’” was insufficient to meet amount-in-controversy requirement where “the complaint itself

                                  14   contained no allegations that could justify the same.”).

                                  15           Accordingly, the Court finds that Mr. Eskenasy’s complaint does not adequately plead

                                  16   federal subject matter jurisdiction.

                                  17           D.      Failure to State a Claim
                                  18           Even if Mr. Eskenasy could amend the complaint to adequately plead federal subject

                                  19   matter jurisdiction, the complaint does not plausibly allege any viable claims for relief. According

                                  20   to the complaint, Mr. Eskenasy “does not presently allege” that LinkedIn or Microsoft “copied

                                  21   ChefreyOS,” “stole [p]laintiff’s work,” “retaliated against [p]laintiff,” “intentionally suppressed

                                  22   [p]laintiff’s visibility,” or “shadow-banned” plaintiff. See Dkt. No. 1 ¶¶ 190-197. Rather, the

                                  23   complaint is based on Mr. Eskenasy’s speculation that he may have a claim because “the preserved

                                  24   record raises a serious authorship/provenance concern” and that LinkedIn’s and Microsoft’s

                                  25   records are “necessary to determine what happened.” Id. ¶ 8. The complaint does not identify Mr.

                                  26   Eskenasy’s work at issue nor which LinkedIn materials raise “authorship” concerns. Mr.

                                  27   Eskenasy pleads no facts showing that he is entitled to an evidence preservation order or other

                                  28   relief. See Twombly, 550 U.S. at 555 (“Factual allegations must be enough to raise a right to relief
                                                                                          5
                                          Case 5:26-cv-06047-VKD             Document 5         Filed 07/08/26    Page 6 of 7




                                   1   above the speculative level . . . .” (citation omitted)).

                                   2           To the extent that Mr. Eskenasy brings this action because he is having difficulty accessing

                                   3   his LinkedIn account, he likewise fails to state a claim. The complaint identifies no obligations,

                                   4   contractual or otherwise, that any defendant owes to Mr. Eskenasy and breached. See Baldwin

                                   5   Kennedy v. Meta Platforms Inc., No. 23-cv-06615-HSG, 2025 WL 1935433, at *1, *4 (N.D. Cal.

                                   6   June 5, 2025) (dismissing claims asserting various theories, where plaintiff alleged defendant

                                   7   failed to help her restore access to her Facebook account and denied her request for a verification

                                   8   checkmark on her Instagram account, but identified no duty owed by defendant); King v.

                                   9   Facebook, Inc., No. 19-cv-01987-WHO, 2019 WL 6493968, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 3, 2019)

                                  10   (dismissing breach of contract claim against Facebook where plaintiff failed to identify the

                                  11   specific provision at issue), aff’d, 845 F. App’x 691 (9th Cir. 2021).

                                  12           Accordingly, the Court finds that Mr. Eskenasy fails to plausibly allege a claim for relief.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   III.    CONCLUSION
                                  14           For the reasons discussed above, Mr. Eskenasy’s complaint fails to establish federal

                                  15   subject matter jurisdiction and fails to state a claim for relief. Given the nature of Mr. Eskenasy’s

                                  16   claims, the Court is skeptical that Mr. Eskenasy could amend the complaint to establish federal

                                  17   subject matter jurisdiction or to state a plausible, non-speculative claim for relief against

                                  18   defendants. However, in view of Mr. Eskenasy’s pro se status, the Court will give him an

                                  19   opportunity to file an amended complaint if he believes he can cure these defects. See Akhtar v.

                                  20   Mesa, 698 F.3d 1202, 1212 (9th Cir. 2012). The amended complaint must be filed no later than

                                  21   August 7, 2026 and must include the caption and civil case number used in this order, Case No.

                                  22   26-cv-06047-VKD, and the words “FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT” on the first page. Mr.

                                  23   Eskenasy is advised that the first amended complaint will supersede the original complaint, the

                                  24   latter being treated thereafter as non-existent. Ramirez v. Cnty. of San Bernardino, 806 F.3d 1002,

                                  25   1008 (9th Cir. 2015).

                                  26           If Mr. Eskenasy fails to file an amended complaint in time, or if the amended complaint

                                  27   fails to cure the defects described in this order, the Court may issue an order reassigning the case

                                  28   to a district judge with a recommendation that the complaint be dismissed for lack of federal
                                                                                           6
                                          Case 5:26-cv-06047-VKD            Document 5          Filed 07/08/26    Page 7 of 7




                                   1   subject matter jurisdiction and failure to state a claim for relief.

                                   2           Additionally, Mr. Eskenasy is informed that the Pro Se Program at the San Jose

                                   3   Courthouse provides free information and limited-scope legal advice to self-represented litigants

                                   4   in federal cases. Information regarding the Pro Se Program can be found at

                                   5   https://cand.uscourts.gov/representing-yourself/federal-pro-se-program-san-jose-courthouse.

                                   6   Appointments may be scheduled by calling 408-297-1480. Mr. Eskenasy is also encouraged to

                                   7   obtain a copy of the Handbook for Pro Se Litigants, available at https://cand.uscourts.gov/pro-se-

                                   8   handbook/.

                                   9           IT IS SO ORDERED.

                                  10   Dated: July 8, 2026
